title: Why does array indexing start at 0?
question: In most programming languages, arrays are 0-indexed. Which of the following best explains why?
options: It's arbitrary — a historical convention with no technical reason.
An index represents an offset from the first element's memory address. The first element is 0 offsets away.
Loops are faster when they start at 0.
explanation: Array indexing maps directly to memory offsets. If arr starts at memory address M, then arr[i] = M + (i × element_size). The first element is at M + 0 = M, so its index is 0. This is why 0-indexing is natural and efficient.

title: When to use a sliding window?
question: Which of these problems is best solved with a sliding window technique?
options: Find the maximum element in an unsorted array.
Find the longest substring with at most K distinct characters.
Check if two strings are anagrams of each other.
explanation: Sliding window is ideal for contiguous subarray/substring problems where you're looking for an optimal range. 'Longest substring with K distinct chars' involves expanding and shrinking a window over contiguous elements — a perfect fit.

title: What happens without a base case?
question: A recursive function without a valid base case will:
options: Run indefinitely and eventually cause a stack overflow error.
explanation: Each recursive call adds a new frame to the call stack. Without a base case, the function never stops calling itself. The stack grows until it exceeds its memory limit — causing a StackOverflow error.

title: Array vs Linked List: insertion at head
question: Inserting an element at the beginning (head) of a data structure — which is faster?
options: Array — it's contiguous in memory, so it's always faster.
Linked List — O(1) to update the head pointer.
explanation: In an array, inserting at index 0 requires shifting all existing elements right — O(n). In a linked list, you simply create a new node and point it to the current head — O(1). This is one of the key trade-offs between the two structures.

title: The mutable default argument trap
question:
What does this function print on the second call?

def append_to(x, lst=[]):
    lst.append(x)
    return lst

append_to(1)
append_to(2)
options: Error — default args can't be lists.
explanation: Default argument values are evaluated once when the function is defined, not each time it's called. The list [] is created once and reused. After two calls, it contains [1, 2]. The fix: use None as default and create the list inside the function body.

title: Identify the Time Complexity
explanation: Two nested loops, each running n times independently, result in n × n = n² total iterations. This is O(n²) — quadratic time complexity.

title: Why is binary search O(log n)?
question: Binary search on a sorted array of 1024 elements needs at most how many comparisons?
explanation: Binary search halves the search space with each comparison. Starting at 1024: 512 → 256 → 128 → 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1. That's 10 steps. Since 2^10 = 1024, the complexity is O(log₂ n) — logarithmic time.
